title: "Visualization of Correlations between possible predictors"

I realized that my previous EDA did not account for the different codes each variable took. For example, a lot of the time, "6" or "9" would be used to denote a skipped response. Thus, the vast majority of correlations in my previous plot was driven by natural groupings of people who would skip something (e.g. people who are non-smokers, or people who exercise at least once a week). 

To fix this, I painstakingly went through all 114 pages of the data dictionary and assigned each variable to a "class", which represents the type of response, of which there are only a few (thank god). Moreover, I also annotated the value of "skipped responses". That is, if a participant skipped a question, what value did it take? This varied across different questions, so I also included it as trailing numbers after the "class". I then used this information to clean the data and organize the columns into important classes (e.g. categorical variables, numeric variables, etc). 

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The cleaned data and assigned classes are found below."
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)

pumf <- read_csv(
    "/Users/jerrychen/Desktop/StatsFinalProject/Datasets/CSV/Data_Données/pumf_cchs.csv"
)

# NA: Not useful (only takes 1 value)
# Cat: Categorical in nature, no ordering
# Ord: Categorical but has natural ordering
# YN: Yes/No, where Yes = 1, No = 2
# YNC: Yes/No, where Yes = 1 and No = 0
# YNDK: Yes/No/Don't Know, where Yes = 1, No = 2, Don't know = 3
# Num: Numeric variable
# Numbers after class: Corresponds to skipped option. Typically, ending with "6" means valid skip, whereas "9" just means normal skip
# For example, "Num 996 999" would mean the input is numeric (e.g. minutes for commute), and any skipped option is 996 and 999
classes <- c(
  "VERDATE" = "NA",
  "REFPER" = "NA", # page 3
  "ADM_RNO" = "NA", # page 3
  "COLMODE" = "Cat 6", # page 3
  "COLMODEY" = "Cat 6", # page 3
  "COLMODEP" = "Cat 6 9", # page 3
  "GEOGPRV" = "Cat", # page 3
  "GEODGHR4" = "Cat", # page 3
  "DHHDGHSZ" = "YN 9", # page 3, 1 = Yes = Lives alone, 2 = No = Doesn't live alone, Question: "Do you live alone?"
  "EDDVH3" = "Cat 9", # page 3
  "DHHGAGE" = "Ord", # page 3
  "DHH_SEX" = "Cat", # page 3
  "DOMAC" = "NA", # page 3
  "MAC_05" = "YN 6 9", # page 3

# General classes (just getting the root class)
general_classes <- sub(" .*", "", classes)

# All variables that are not useless
non_NA <- names(classes)[classes != "NA"]

cleaned_data <- lapply(non_NA, FUN = function(column) {

  # Vector of strings, separated by a space
  complete_class <- str_split_1(classes[column], " ")

  # Either NA, Cat, Ord, YN, YNC, YNDK, or Num
  root_class <- complete_class[1]

  # If the user skipped, what number would it be? 
  skipped_options <- as.numeric(setdiff(complete_class, root_class))

  cleaned_vector <- pumf[[column]]

  # Replacing all skipped options to NA
  cleaned_vector[cleaned_vector %in% skipped_options] <- NA

  # Adjusting for each class

  # If categorical, then just return the same vector but factorized
  if (root_class == "Cat") {
    return(factor(cleaned_vector))
  }

  # If categorical with ordering, or numeric, or YNC, then just return the same vector
  if (root_class %in% c("Ord", "Num", "YNC")) {
    return(cleaned_vector)
  }
  # If YN, then return the same vector but replacing all 2's with 0's. This is done to match "No" to 0 and "Yes" to 1 for consistency
  if (root_class == "YN") {
    cleaned_vector[cleaned_vector == 2] <- 0
    return(cleaned_vector)
  }

  # If YNDK, then return the same vector but replacing 2's with 0's and 3's with 2's, so we have No = 0, Yes = 1, Don't know = 2. Then factor it
  if (root_class == "YNDK") {
    cleaned_vector[cleaned_vector == 2] <- 0
    cleaned_vector[cleaned_vector == 3] <- 2
    return(factor(cleaned_vector))
  }

}) |>
  setNames(non_NA) |>
  as_tibble()

# Classes that are purely numeric (not factored)
numeric_classes <- names(general_classes)[general_classes %in% c("Ord", "YN", "YNC", "Num")]
```

Using this cleaned data, I then repeated the same analysis as before. Since I can't use variables that are factored (i.e. categorical variabels) in this analysis, I left them out in the heatmap. 

The following heatmap was constructed as follows: Each row and column represents one of the predictors from the CCHS dataset (i.e. the elements of the vector above). The intersection between them represents the correlation between the two predictors (red = closer to 1, blue = closer to -1). Grey cells represent mutually exclusive categories (e.g. "Number of cigarettes smoked" and "Health in Non-smokers"). For example, the diagonal is all 1 because the correlation between a predictor and itself is always 1. I first did this across all numeric predictors. I then "clustered" the values, which basically means sorting the rows and columns based on how similar they are to each other. This creates "clusters" of predictors that share similar values to each other, which will look like chunks of red and blue. 

![full_predictor_heatmap](predictor_corr.png)

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "All of my code is here if you guys wanna see it. "
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
library(viridis)
library(circlize)
library(ComplexHeatmap)

# This is the file above containing cleaned data 
source(file = "/Users/jerrychen/Desktop/StatsFinalProject/data_cleaning.R", echo = FALSE)

# Heatmap: Predictor x Predictor, coloured by correlation
visualize_correlation_matrix <- function(df, column_ids) {
  subset <- df[, column_ids]

  # pairwise.complete.obs will just remove NA values for any two pairs when computing correlation
  corr_mat <- cor(subset, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

  rownames(corr_mat) <- dict[rownames(corr_mat)]

  cols = c("#2166ac",
             "#4393c3",
             "#92c5de", 
             "#d1e5f0",
             "#f7f7f7",
             "#fddbc7",
             "#f4a582",
             "#d6604d",
             "#b2182b")
  sim_col <- circlize::colorRamp2(seq(-1, 1, length.out = length(cols)), cols)

  ht <- Heatmap(
    corr_mat,
    col = sim_col,
    show_row_dend = FALSE,
    show_column_dend = FALSE
  )

  png(
    "predictor_corr.png", 
    width = 40,
    height = 40,
    units = "in",
    res = 250
  )
  
  draw(ht, heatmap_legend_side = "left")
  
  dev.off()

  return(rownames(corr_mat)[row_order(draw(ht))])
  
}

visualize_correlation_matrix(cleaned_data, numeric_classes)
```
